kurz: Why, for the same average return, the shape of the payoff decides the outcome, and how to build a portfolio accordingly.

bloecke.md:
The expected value states what comes out on average. It says nothing about how this average comes about, and that determines whether a position is bearable.

There are two basic shapes. A payoff is **concave** if it brings many small gains and a rare large loss. This includes option writing, credit risk premiums, subordinated loans, guarantees and any business in which you collect a premium. A **convex** payoff is the mirror image, with many small losses and a rare large gain. An investor who pays a premium is buying convexity.

Both shapes can have the same expected value. They differ in what becomes of one euro over twenty years. Wealth develops multiplicatively, so a single catastrophic year cannot be made up for by nineteen good years.

Portfolio A is concave. In 19 out of 20 years it returns plus 7%, in the twentieth minus 90%. The arithmetic mean is (19 × 7 − 90) / 20 = 2.15% a year.

Portfolio B is convex. In 19 out of 20 years it returns minus 2%, in the twentieth plus 82%. The arithmetic mean is (19 × (−2) + 82) / 20 = 2.20% a year.

After 20 years, €10,000 becomes:

- Portfolio A: 1.07^19 × 0.10 = 0.3617, that is, €3,617 or −4.96% a year
- Portfolio B: 0.98^19 × 1.82 = 1.2398, that is, €12,398 or +1.08% a year

With almost the same expected value, the results differ by a factor of 3.4. The order of the years plays no role here; all that matters is the shape of the payoff.

bloecke.erklaerung: The formula describes the Jensen term. For a convex payoff function, the second derivative is positive and so is the term, which means that fluctuation increases the expected result. For a concave payoff, the term is negative, and the same fluctuation lowers the expected result. The formula sums up Taleb's thesis. It holds regardless of whether the fluctuation can be predicted.

bloecke.beispiel: In the schematic example, f(x) = x², and S fluctuates between 8 and 12 with a mean of 10 and a variance of 4. Then f(E[S]) = 100, but E[f(S)] = (64 + 144) / 2 = 104. The difference of 4 is exactly ½ × 2 × 4. These 4 points come from convexity alone, without any forecast.

bloecke.md:
## The barbell strategy

Uncertainty benefits a convex position and harms a concave one. This leads to a portfolio form that Taleb calls the **barbell**. It consists of a very safe main part and a small, deliberately risky remainder, with nothing in between. In *Antifragile* (2012), Taleb gives as one variant around 90% very safe and around 10% highly speculative, broadly diversified. The split is meant as an example. It illustrates the basic idea of limiting the downside and leaving the upside open.

The middle is avoided because it carries risks that cannot be quantified. Its return is not the reason for this. A mixed fund with 60% equities and 40% corporate bonds of medium creditworthiness looks balanced. In periods of stress, however, both parts fall at the same time, and nobody knows in advance by how much. With the barbell this is known, because you cannot lose more than the risky part.

bloecke.titel: Three portfolios under the same market movement
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation: the safe part is assumed to yield 2.5%, the convex part reacts fourfold to the market, and its loss is limited to the amount invested. The middle is calculated with a safe bond portion; with corporate bonds as in the text, it would be lower in sharp market declines. The barbell has a floor at −7.75% and in return participates less in good years.

bloecke.md:
The curves show the advantage of the barbell and its price. For market movements below about plus 6%, the barbell is ahead of the middle; above that, it falls behind. It already falls behind the fully invested portfolio from plus 3.75%. In a year with plus 50%, it reaches 22.25% instead of 50%. With the barbell, you therefore deliberately give up part of the returns of good years in order to have a floor in bad years.

At minus 25%, the barbell's curve has a kink. From there on, the convex part is completely lost, and further market losses cost nothing more. The value of the construction lies in this kink and not in the leverage effect.

## Optionality without bought options

**Optionality** means the right to decide later without being obliged to do so. A warrant is the most expensive and shortest-lived way of obtaining it. Most sources of optionality in a private portfolio cost part of the ongoing return rather than a premium in the sense of time value, and they never expire.

bloecke.titel: Five sources of optionality in the portfolio
zeilen: Liquidity (instant-access savings, money market ETF)
Real interest after tax, often negative
Right to buy at any price level; never expires
Misused as a timing instrument instead of being held as a reserve
Broad diversification instead of selection
You also hold the losers
The few extreme winners are automatically included
Spreading across 40 funds from the same region remains a cluster risk
No securities-backed loan, no Lombard loan
Forgoing leverage in good years
No forced sale at the low; the decision stays with the investor
An arranged overdraft or a clause requiring additional payments also acts like leverage
Short lock-in periods
Slightly less interest or bonus
Exit possible if the situation changes
Endowment policies and closed-ended AIFs tie up money for decades
Own qualifications, second source of income
Time, money spent on learning
Loss limited, upside open; uncorrelated with the portfolio
Booked as consumption instead of investment

bloecke.md:
## Via negativa

Taleb's second practical principle comes from theology. It states that what does harm is known with greater certainty than what helps. Applied to a portfolio, this means first removing sources of loss instead of searching for sources of gain. The effect of removing is certain, the effect of searching is not.

Costs are the biggest single lever, and the calculation is simple. It assumes €10,000, a 7% gross return and 30 years. With ongoing charges of 0.20%, €71,968 remains; with 1.50%, only €49,840. The difference of €22,128 is around a third of the final wealth. It arises from 1.3 percentage points a year, calculated before tax and without an initial charge.

The second subtraction concerns funds that you no longer see at all. Of the active US equity funds that existed 20 years earlier, 37.29% still existed in mid-2025. Around 63% had been closed or merged. Of the European equity funds, 58% were still in existence after 10 years. Rankings, five-star ratings and twenty-year retrospectives therefore show only an excerpt that is missing the entire left tail of the distribution, that is, the worst results.

## Dealing with black swans

According to Taleb, a black swan has three characteristics. It lies outside well-founded expectations, it has extreme effects, and in hindsight it is explained as if it had been foreseeable. The first characteristic is the decisive one. This is why Taleb himself explicitly did not classify the coronavirus pandemic as a black swan. A pandemic was to be expected, had been modelled and was described in emergency plans. It was a white swan that had been ignored.

It follows that you do without forecasts instead of searching for better ones. The track record of professional forecasts is clear. From 2018 to 2025, the consensus estimate of Wall Street strategists for the S&P 500 was within plus or minus 10 percentage points in only one of eight years. The biggest miss came in 2022. Plus 3.9% was expected, and the result was minus 19.4%, a deviation of 23.3 percentage points. For 2024, the consensus expected plus 2%, and the outcome was plus 23%.

Dealing with black swans means building the portfolio so that the forecast plays no role. To do this, you limit the loss, keep your participation in open-ended gains and make use of a long investment horizon.

bloecke.titel: Best and worst DAX result by holding period
bloecke.unter: Source: Deutsches Aktieninstitut, return triangle covering 50 years, as of 31 December 2025. With a longer holding period, the negative results disappear while the positive ones remain, and so time creates an asymmetry without any derivatives at all.

bloecke.md: From a holding period of 15 years, there has historically been no negative result in the DAX. At 20 years, the worst case was 3.3%, the average 8.4% and the best case 15.2% a year. This is not a guarantee, because fifty years of a single index are a narrow sample, and the figures are calculated before costs and taxes. Nevertheless, a long holding period is the cheapest convexity available. It costs only patience and the ability not to have to sell.

bloecke.unter: Only the top left field is convex. The bottom right field looks best for years, until the rare large loss occurs.

felder.text: Broadly diversified equity portfolio without borrowing, a small admixture of venture capital, your own qualifications. Many small disappointments, rare big hits.
Leveraged single bet, shares bought on credit, property with 100% financing. Open-ended profit potential, but the loss can exceed your own capital.
Instant-access savings, short-dated German federal bonds, fixed-term deposits as the safe part of the barbell. Neither opportunity nor catastrophe.
Option writing, subordinated loans, credit-linked notes, guarantees. The premium comes regularly; the loss is rare and large.

bloecke.md:
The shape of a payoff says nothing about its price. A convex profile bought at too high a price is a bad bet, even if the loss is limited.

In Germany, convexity is mostly sold in the form of warrants, knock-outs or certificates. Legally, these are bearer bonds (Inhaberschuldverschreibungen) of the issuing bank. They are not segregated fund assets (Sondervermögen) and are not covered by deposit protection. If the issuer becomes insolvent, there is therefore a risk of total loss, regardless of how the underlying has performed. The standard example is the Lehman insolvency in September 2008. In addition, there are the bid-ask spread, the warrant premium, financing costs and management fees. As with funds, the mandatory key information document (KID) under the PRIIPs Regulation shows the total costs in euros and as a percentage, and the bank must disclose the costs in aggregated form before the purchase (Section 63(7) WpHG, Securities Trading Act).

For CFDs, leverage caps for retail clients have applied since 1 August 2018, from 30:1 on major currency pairs to 2:1 on crypto assets. ESMA had agreed on them on 27 March 2018; since 1 August 2019, in Germany they have been based on a general administrative order issued by BaFin (Federal Financial Supervisory Authority). In addition, there is a mandatory close-out at 50% of the minimum margin and negative balance protection. The obligation to make additional payments (Nachschusspflicht) has been ruled out for retail investors in Germany since 2017. A total loss of the amount invested thus explicitly remains possible. The mandatory risk warning from providers typically states that 70% to 85% of accounts lose money.

- Losses from the sale of individual shares end up in the **share loss pot** (Aktienverlusttopf) under Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG (Income Tax Act) and can only be offset against gains from the sale of shares. If the risky arm of the barbell consists of individual shares, its losses are tied up in this pot and are difficult to offset. With a broad ETF, the same losses end up in the general loss pot (allgemeiner Verlusttopf).
- For **derivative transactions** (Termingeschäfte), there used to be a limit of €20,000 a year on loss offsetting (Section 20(6) sentence 5 EStG, former version), and an equally high limit for bad debt losses (sentence 6, former version). The Annual Tax Act 2024 (Jahressteuergesetz) of 2 December 2024 abolished both without replacement, applicable in all open cases (Section 52(28) EStG). Older guides are out of date on this point.
- Under the **FIFO rule** (Section 20(4) sentence 7 EStG), in a partial sale the units bought first are deemed to have been sold first, per securities account and without any right to choose. Investors who want to choose between older and newer units need separate securities accounts or sub-accounts. This choice is bought optionality, and its price is somewhat more administrative effort.
- Investors with securities accounts at several banks can request a **loss certificate** (Verlustbescheinigung) under Section 43a(3) sentence 4 EStG in order to offset losses at one bank against gains at another in their tax return. The request must reach the bank by 15 December of the current year (sentence 5) and is irrevocable. If the deadline passes, this option lapses for the current year, and the bank carries the loss forward to the next year.
- Ongoing income is taxed at 25% plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge, that is, 26.375% in total (Section 32d(1) EStG; Section 4 SolzG 1995, Solidarity Surcharge Act), after deducting the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 per person or €2,000 for joint assessment (Section 20(9) EStG).

In the model above, the convex arm loses everything in a market decline of 25% or more, and the portfolio then stands at −7.75%. Suppose this happens in 3 out of 10 years, and in the remaining 7 years the market does not move at all. In those years the portfolio earns only the 2.25% of the safe arm. The calculation is:

0.9225³ × 1.0225⁷ = 0.7851 × 1.1685 = 0.9174

After ten years, 91.74% of the initial capital is left, which corresponds to −0.86% a year. That is what this construction costs in a decade without upward swings. Convexity is therefore not free; it is a bet that the big movements will come and that you stay solvent until then.

Robust means surviving a shock unchanged. **Antifragile** means becoming better through a shock. This requires the loss to be limited and the upside to be open-ended. A safety buffer alone makes a portfolio robust, but not antifragile.

mitnehmen: Two positions with almost the same expected value can be a factor of three apart after twenty years, because the shape of the payoff decides the outcome.
Convex positions gain from fluctuation and concave ones lose from it, even if nobody can predict the fluctuation.
The barbell limits the loss and leaves the upside open; its noticeable price is lower participation in good years.
Optionality in the portfolio comes from liquidity, broad diversification, doing without credit and short lock-in periods, without having to buy leveraged products for it.
According to the principle of via negativa, cutting costs, avoiding lock-in and ruling out ruin work with certainty, whereas picking winners only might work.

begriffe.text: Property of a payoff in which the loss is limited and the upside is open-ended. Convex positions benefit from fluctuation; formally, E[f(S)] lies above f(E[S]).

Also called a barbell. Portfolio structure consisting of a very safe main part and a small, deliberately risky remainder, with no investments in the medium risk class. Taleb cites a split of roughly 90 to 10 as one variant.
Principle of first removing sources of harm instead of looking for sources of gain. It rests on the fact that what does harm is known with greater certainty than what helps.
Property of a system of becoming better through stress. This is to be distinguished from robustness, in which a system merely survives a shock unchanged.
Event outside well-founded expectations with an extreme impact, which in hindsight is explained as if it had been foreseeable. A foreseeable event that was ignored does not count as one.
